extracted.intended_audience: learned theologians, clergy, and students of Christian doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative and interpretive guidance for evaluating liturgical consecration practices, doctrines of the soul (immortality, purgatory, eternal punishment), and accounts of spirits/possession in Christian Scripture and tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency and significance of rites in consecration
rubrics_metrics.description: the ceremonies, words, and gestures, be both decent, and significant, or at least conformable to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rituals should be simple, decent, rational, and appropriate to the occasion. Examples: Moses anointed and used oil to consecrate the Tabernacle and vessels; Aaron and his sons were washed with water (not exorcised water), clothed, and anointed. Anti-patterns: unnecessary processions, exorcised water, asperges me, or borrowing impertinent words from other occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of exorcisms and inappropriate accretions in consecration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consecrations in Scripture were performed without exorcisms or superfluous applications (e.g., exorcised water, spittle ceremonies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce practices (such as spittle applied to the nose with phrases like 'in odorem suavitatis') that lack scriptural or authoritative justification. Use only ceremonies that are conformable to the action and have reasonable authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liturgical acts that effect consecration (washing, clothing, anointing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Washing with water, putting on garments, and anointing with oil constitute proper acts of consecration as seen in Moses' consecration of Aaron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on simple cleansing and adorning rites that signify sanctification to present servants to God; such acts are sufficient without additional exorcistic adjuncts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret Scripture in context and by comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages that at first sight support an idea must be compared with other texts (e.g., Job 14) and interpreted in the full scriptural context before drawing doctrinal conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh multiple passages against one another; avoid building doctrine on isolated texts that admit divergent readings. The literal sense must be tested by the wider scriptural harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer natural immortality of the soul from isolated texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture does not plainly prove that the soul separated from the body naturally lives eternally without special grace; many texts admit alternative interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages like Ecclesiastes 12:7 and other texts can be read as indicating God's knowledge rather than human certainty, or as referring to resurrection by grace. Treat texts that might suggest universal natural immortality with caution and look for doctrinal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful interpretation of 'everlasting' language in punishment texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Words such as 'everlasting fire', 'everlasting torments', and 'the worm of conscience never dyeth' need not prove individual, unending torment; they may mean a perpetual state of punishment maintained by successive sinners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider readings where the fire or punishment continues (i.e., never lacks sinners to punish) without implying each individual's endless conscious torment. Avoid forcing 'everlasting' to mean the same as natural immortality of the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate resurrection-to-life from resurrection-to-punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: St. Paul’s account of the resurrection (1 Cor. 15) describes bodies raised to eternal life (incorruptible, spiritual); there is no clear scriptural basis that reprobate bodies will be identical to the elect's spiritual bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit resurrection passages (1 Cor. 15; Luke 20) to judge the nature of post-resurrection bodies and estates; do not assume reprobates will share the elect's spiritual, incorruptible condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using rhetorical or honorific acts as proof of post-mortem intermediary states
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts such as David’s fasting for Saul and Abner are honors or expressions of grief/benefit, not evidence that the dead occupy an intermediate place (purgatory) where prayers change their state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe public mourning or fasting as implying belief in a third place for souls. Distinguish cultural/ritual motives (honour, personal consolation) from doctrinal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate 'the world to come' with purgatory
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'world to come' should be understood within a tripartite scriptural scheme (old world, present world until judgment, and the everlasting world from judgment onward); it is inconsistent to make the 'world to come' into a temporal purgatorial state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure exegesis of phrases like 'neither in this world, nor in the world to come' (Matt. 12:32) coheres with the scriptural cosmology; avoid reassigning eschatological categories to support purgatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat ambiguous passages (e.g., baptism for the dead) with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 Cor. 15:29 ('baptized for the dead') admits multiple interpretations (metaphorical baptism of penance, vicarious surety-baptism); it should not be used decisively to prove purgatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interpretations consistent with the rest of Scripture and avoid building paradoxical doctrines on passages that are obscure or metaphorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret parabolic and judicial language by overall context
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical judicial sayings (e.g., Matt. 5:25 about prison until the utmost farthing) are to be read as moral/eschatological admonitions, not as literal descriptions of post-mortem legal courts and offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read such sayings with their immediate context (law interpretation, moral correction) and avoid importing a judicial structure of multiple post-mortem courts as proof of purgatorial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not create multiple eschatological courts from intra-Jewish legal categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiating sins and punishments in Matt. 5:22 is not evidence for separate post-mortem courts (judges, council) with different punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand Christ’s intensification of the law as moral teaching; interpret references to judgment collectively (Christ and apostles) rather than as separate afterlife tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deriving invocation of saints or post-mortem remissions from misplaced texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Verses like Luke 16:9 (making friends with unrighteous mammon) and Luke 23:42 ('Lord remember me') are misused when taken as direct proof of invocation of the dead or remissions after death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret such verses in their charitable/ethical or miraculous context (giving to the poor; Christ’s promise to the penitent thief), not as liturgical or doctrinal endorsements of post-mortem intercession or purgatorial remission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check grammatical and lexical readings before doctrinal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts 2:24 ('loosed the pains of death') has been read as a descent into purgatory, but careful reading (Beza's 'bands' vs 'pains') and referent analysis show the text concerns Christ, not souls in purgatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exegesis must attend to grammar, lexical possibilities, and correct referents; avoid doctrinal leaps based on doubtful translations or strained readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read metaphors of refining/fire in eschatological context
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 Cor. 3 (work tried by fire) and Zachariah’s refining imagery refer to the Day of Judgment and the world’s renewal rather than an intermediate purgatorial fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map metaphors to prophetic/apostolic eschatological frameworks; prefer readings that locate the purging/refining imagery at final judgment rather than in an independent purgatorial state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain apparitions and visions by natural perceptual causes first
rubrics_metrics.description: Impressions on the organs of sight by lucid bodies or aftereffects of pressure produce imaginations, memories, and dreams; these explain many apparitions that ancients called daemons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before positing incorporeal beings, consider physiological and psychological explanations (sensory impressions, imagination, dreams, sickness). The text argues imagination is often mistaken for real external entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward attributing inner anomalies to independent spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancients often treated transient inner images as external 'daemons'; this is a category mistake — internal phantasms need not be independent or material spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reading personal or cultural oddities (madness, prophetic utterance, epileptic seizures) as evidence of inhabited incorporeal spirits; interpret them as states of the person unless positive evidence indicates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'possession' language metaphorically where apt
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Satan entered into him' (Judas) may mean hostile intention or wicked cogitations, not literal entrance of a being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider metaphorical/psychological readings of possession language; prefer explanations that render the phrase as describing internal dispositions or intentions unless the narrative insists on supernatural agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow non-material bodies as bodily entities (nuanced notion of 'spirit')
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture’s use of 'spirit' does not necessarily imply immateriality; 'spiritual bodies' or 'air' can be bodies of a subtler sort, not 'flesh and bone'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about what 'spirit' denotes in each text; do not automatically equate 'spirit' with purely immaterial substances — consider corporeality in a subtler sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that Scripture does not aim to settle all natural philosophical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some matters (e.g., why Christ did not reveal all natural causes) are more curious than necessary for salvation; Scripture may leave natural explanations to human reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not fault Scripture for not teaching every natural/scientific truth; theological interpretation should respect the bounds of salvific revelation versus natural philosophy.
